gallery.title: File:1784 Bocage Map of the City of Athens in Ancient Greece - Geographicus - AthensPlan2-white-1793.jpg
gallery.description: This lovely little map or city plan of Athens in Ancient Greece, was prepared by M. Barbie de Bocage in 1784 for the “Travels of Anarcharsis”.  Athens, capital of the Athenian Empire, was the heart of Ancient Greek culture and the quintessential Ancient Greek city state.  This plan of Athens, based on excavations and ancient sources offers impressive and accurate detail.

gallery.title: File:1785 Bocage Map of Athens and Environs, including Piraeus, in Ancient Greece - Geographicus - Athens-white-1793.jpg
gallery.description: This lovely little map or city plan of Athens and Environs in Ancient Greece, was prepared by M. Barbie de Bocage in 1784 for the “Travels of Anarcharsis”.  Athens, capital of the Athenian Empire, was the heart of Ancient Greek culture and the quintessential Ancient Greek city state.  It was here that Greek philosophy and literature as well as the concept of democracy first evolved. This plan of Athens, based on excavations and ancient sources offers impressive and accurate detail.  Includes the Long Walls, build to protect merchants as they passed from Athens to the port city of Piraeus.  Also includes the Academy of Plato.

gallery.title: File:Plato's Academy, Athens.jpg
gallery.description: The Academy (Ancient Greek: Ἀκαδημία) was founded by Plato (428/427 BC – 348/347 BC) in ca. 387 BC in Athens. Aristotle (384 BC – 322 BC) studied there for twenty years (367 BC – 347 BC) before founding his own school, the Lyceum. The Academy persisted throughout the Hellenistic period as a skeptical school, until coming to an end after the death of Philo of Larissa in 83 BC. Although philosophers continued to teach Plato's philosophy in Athens throughout the Roman era, it was not until 410 AD that a revived Academy was established as a center for Neoplatonism, persisting until 529 AD when it was finally closed by Justinian I.

gallery.title: File:Libra point, Xi platonic.png
gallery.description:
Equinox at the Libra Point
This image illustrates the relationship between the ecliptic, the celestial equator, and the tropics in the context of the equinox associated with the Libra Point. The figure is a parallelogram with three main lines:
Top line: Represents the Tropic of Cancer, associated with the June solstice.
Middle line: Corresponds to the Celestial Equator, the projection of Earth's equator onto the celestial sphere.
Bottom line: Represents the Tropic of Capricorn, linked to the December solstice.
The intersection of the ecliptic (green line) with the celestial equator (red line) marks the Libra Point, corresponding to one of the equinoxes. In the image, the ecliptic crosses the celestial equator in a downward direction, indicating the September equinox.
The arrows in the illustration indicate the following movements:
Gray arrow on the celestial equator: Direction of the celestial equator’s movement.
Gray arrow on the ecliptic: Represents the direction of the precession of the equinoxes.
At the top and bottom of the image, the symbols for Cancer (♋) and Capricorn (♑) represent the Sun’s positions during the solstices. In the center, the Libra symbol (♎) marks the equinox.

This diagram helps visualize the relationship between fundamental celestial movements and the dynamics of the equinoxes within the celestial coordinate system.
